comparator.sourceNotes: The English-taught route has 60 EC of first-year media study, 24 EC of common second-year courses plus three 12 EC choices, and 42 EC of open electives plus an 18 EC thesis seminar. The example selects Film Studies in each choice group.

routeSelection.basis: The official programme page lists Film Studies before Television and Cross-Media Culture. The comparison illustrates the Film course in each of the three 12 EC groups.

core: Film, television and audiovisual-media history, theory and analysis
Media aesthetics, representation, storytelling and cultural meaning
Media research methods, criticism, academic writing and independent inquiry
Media, society, audiences and cultural transformation
adjacent: Film studies, visual storytelling and cinema culture
Contemporary media, digital platforms and cultural identity
questions: How do audiovisual forms create meaning and shape everyday experience?
How do media histories, institutions and technologies transform culture and society?
How can film, television and digital media be researched, criticised and produced?

alternatives.label: Media history, culture & representation
alternatives.labelReason: Film, documentary, television and media history anchor the option. Historical and social research support the study of cultural change and representation.
alternatives.concept: Study how film, television and other media represent social groups and shape public life. Combine audiovisual analysis and documentary work with research in cultural history and sociology.
progression: Introductory film, literary study and social inquiry support documentary, television, media criticism and historical research.

alternatives.label: Film, adaptation & visual storytelling
alternatives.labelReason: Film form and documentary sit alongside adaptation, visual heritage, museums, rhetoric and creative practice.
alternatives.concept: Study how films and other visual forms tell stories. Analyse film adaptations and documentary, then consider how stories and images are interpreted and presented in cultural institutions.
alternatives.distinctness: This option gives more attention to visual heritage, literary sources, rhetoric and the communication of stories. The broader media history option emphasises television, sociology and historical research.
progression: Introductory film, rhetoric, literature and material culture support advanced adaptation, documentary, museum study and creative communication.

alternatives.label: Television, audiences & cross-media culture
alternatives.labelReason: Television and digital media provide the subject matter, with sustained work in rhetoric, social theory and empirical research.
alternatives.concept: Explore how television, film and digital media reach audiences and shape public debate. Combine media analysis and communication with qualitative and statistical research on social behaviour.
alternatives.distinctness: Television and contemporary media connect to social and behavioural research. Persuasion, climate communication and applied rhetoric give this option a stronger focus on audiences and public debate than the two other options.
progression: Introductory film and rhetoric prepare for later television and persuasive communication. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods. Introductory sociology precedes advanced social theory.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Develops empirical research design, measurement, sampling and statistical analysis in a student project.
Investigates political, economic and cultural modernity from 1815 through industrialisation, nationhood and ideological change.
Builds a historical research project on the American century through question design and critical source analysis.
Reads philosophical arguments from ancient and modern traditions to develop contextual interpretation and reasoned critique.
Uses competing theories and philosophical argument to evaluate ethical questions.
Examines how emotions shape knowledge, ethical judgment and social life, offering conceptual tools for interpreting affect.
Introduces sociological explanations of solidarity, inequality, identity and exclusion.
Develops ethically grounded qualitative research design, data collection, analysis and communication.
Examines modern sociological theory through critical perspectives on modernity, exclusion and colonialism.
Uses contemporary social theory to analyse civil society, public spheres, hegemony, solidarity and social movements.
Designs behavioural experiments and interprets and checks multivariable statistical models.
Analyses argument, rhetorical form and delivery, with practice in persuasive communication.
Analyses how grammar, deixis and other linguistic choices shape effects in literary and nonfiction texts.
Examines public communication of climate issues through texts, film, exhibitions, protest art and social media.
Develops and adapts public-speaking, storytelling and debating activities with primary-school children.
Evaluates framing, argument and ethical persuasion, applying these to community-engaged work.
Uses poetry, performance and experimental practice to explore and communicate artistic ideas.
Relates Western visual art from the late medieval period to contemporary practice to religious, political and cultural change.
Interprets artefacts and production practices to study how objects shaped communities and identities across ancient societies.
Examines African visual traditions, their cultural meanings and the interpretation and display of heritage.
Studies Renaissance Italian art and architecture through artistic exchanges across the Mediterranean.
Connects modern and contemporary artworks to museums, exhibitions and the institutions that shape public reception.
Critiques how art historians have interpreted visual culture and constructed the discipline over time.
Uses close reading and genre to interpret fiction, poetry, drama and nonfiction, with an introduction to film adaptation.
Compares major literary works across periods through questions of freedom, gender, community and mortality.
Compares mythic narratives across traditions and studies their transmission and treatment of power, love and gender.
Examines how memoir, travel writing and digital self-presentation construct memory and identity.
Compares how literary narratives and their film adaptations use their different forms to tell stories.
Applies theories of reading and interpretation to a literary research project.
Uses editing, sound, cinematography, narrative and performance to explain how moving images create meaning.
Interprets communication technologies from print and early recording to networks as historical and cultural objects.
Studies power, social history and representation in US television, film and contemporary digital media.
Analyses how media shape ecological understanding and how people represent human and nonhuman relationships.
Investigates race, representation and power through American media and popular culture.
Studies the ethics, aesthetics and history of nonfiction representation and develops practical documentary work.
blocks: Both analyse how narrative, sound and image produce meaning. UvA applies these tools across a wider range of media objects.
Both examine historical changes in media technologies and their cultural effects. UCR studies the material history of media from print to digital networks.
Both include practical documentary production. UvA also covers fiction production and its associated workflows.
Both use close analysis of film form. UCR centres on adaptations, while UvA also uses frameworks such as auteur, genre and spectator theory.
Both develop research design and qualitative interpretation. UCR applies these methods to social questions, while UvA includes methods and sources specific to media.

selection.assessment: Three options cover broad media history and representation, film adaptation and visual storytelling, and cross-media audiences and public communication. Their different emphases are supported by the scheduled courses.

notes.text: UvA requires a dedicated media studies sequence, including a 12 EC production course and an 18 EC research seminar and thesis. UCR offers related study and practice in documentary, media analysis and communication. Its options cover a wider mix of humanities and social science.

audience.programmeDescription: Media and Culture at the University of Amsterdam studies the history, form and cultural role of media. Students learn to analyse and make media and can develop a focus in film or television and cross-media culture.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related study in media history and representation, film adaptation and visual storytelling, or television and audiences. UvA has a dedicated media studies curriculum with a required production course and thesis.
